name: The Republic of Venice
title: Social Hierarchy of the Republic of Venice: From Doge to the Ghetto
period: 1500–1600 (the city of Venice in the 16th century)

tiers.name: The doge
tiers.you: Forty-one electors have chosen you for life and you promulgate the laws, but you may not open a foreign dispatch alone, and after your death inquisitors will judge your acts and may fine your estate.
tiers.kid: The doge was the head of Venice, chosen for life, but the councils kept a close watch on everything he did.
tiers.rise: The doge was elected from among the patricians, usually a man of the inner circle of powerful families. Most ruled until death, but a few were forced out, and in 1355 the Council of Ten condemned Doge Marino Faliero to death for trying to make himself lord of Venice.
tiers.why: The doge was head of state for life.

tiers.name: Patricians
tiers.term: patrizio, nobil homo, case vecchie, case nuove
tiers.you: You were entered in the Golden Book at birth and take your seat in the Great Council at twenty-five; you wear the black toga in office, and you may be sent to govern a mainland city or command a galley for a year.
tiers.kid: Noble men ran the government of Venice together, and their names were written in a register called the Golden Book.
tiers.rise: Birth alone made a patrician: a son of a noble father registered in the Golden Book, but not a son born to a mother of lower status. From 1498 a noble who followed a career in the Church lost his seat, and new families were admitted only rarely, as in 1381 after the War of Chioggia.
tiers.why: The patricians alone sat in the Great Council.

tiers.name: Clergy
tiers.you: You serve one of the city’s parishes; the Republic watches what you preach from the pulpit and may expel you from its lands if you speak against the government.
tiers.kid: Priests, monks and nuns served Venice’s many churches, but the government kept a close eye on what they said.
tiers.rise: From 1498 a noble who chose a career in the Church was barred from the Great Council, so a patrician’s son had to choose between the councils and the clergy.
tiers.why: Catholicism was the state religion, but the Republic kept its clergy in check.

tiers.name: Citizens
tiers.term: cittadini originari, cittadini de intra, cittadini de extra
tiers.you: You were born in Venice to an old Venetian family, so you may serve the Republic as a secretary or notary in the Doge’s Palace, though only the nobles sit in its councils.
tiers.kid: Citizens were the middle rank of Venice: they worked as the state’s secretaries, lawyers and notaries.
tiers.rise: A family were citizens by birth, as natives of Venice or of Venetian families to the third degree, or by a grant on merit: de intra to work within the city, de extra to sail and trade abroad as Venetians. Jews were excluded.
tiers.why: After the Serrata closed the Great Council, the citizens (cittadini) were instituted as a middle order between the nobility and the common people, a place for ambitious families of wealth and distinction.

tiers.name: Common people
tiers.you: You make naval rope or build galleys in the state Arsenal, belong to your trade’s guild, and have no voice in the councils that govern you.
tiers.kid: Most Venetians were fishermen, salt workers, shipbuilders, glassmakers and other workers.
tiers.rise: The Great Council was closed to commoners except in rare emergencies: in 1381 thirty commoners who had given most to the War of Chioggia were made nobles. A family of wealth and distinction could hope to rise into the citizens.
tiers.why: The common people (popolo) were the great majority of the city.

tiers.name: Foreign communities
tiers.you: You are an Orthodox Greek in Venice; you may celebrate your rites only in your community’s own church, San Giorgio dei Greci, built when San Biagio grew too crowded.
tiers.kid: Greeks, Germans, Armenians and Ottoman merchants lived or traded in Venice, and the Greeks had a church of their own.
tiers.rise: A newcomer could be granted Venetian citizenship on merit, to work within the city or to sail and trade as a Venetian; Jews were excluded.
tiers.why: Venetian society counted foreigners as a body of their own, beside the patricians and the citizens.

tiers.name: Jews of the Ghetto
tiers.you: You live in the Ghetto and wear the red cloth that marks you as a Jew; you may run a pawnshop or deal in second-hand goods and pray in your community’s synagogue, but you can never be a citizen of Venice.
tiers.kid: Venice’s Jews had to live in one district, the Ghetto, and wear a red cloth, but they had their own synagogues there.
tiers.rise: Birth decided it: the law excluded Jews from Venetian citizenship, and the Ghetto was their only lawful home in the city.
tiers.why: Jews had no Venetian citizenship and for long no right to live in the city.
